references.text: The immediate context in [ref:Luk 16:10-11|Luke 16:10-11] establishes the principle that faithfulness in small things shows faithfulness in great things, and that whoever is not faithful with unjust wealth will not be entrusted with true riches. Verse 12 continues this reasoning by distinguishing between what belongs to another (what is foreign) and what is one's own.

In the parable of the talents in [ref:Matt 25:21-23|Matthew 25:21-23], the master says to the faithful servants, "You have been faithful over a little; I will set you over much." This illustrates the same principle as in Luke 16:12 – faithfulness with what is entrusted to one (another's property) leads to receiving something of one's own.

In the parable of the minas in [ref:Luk 19:17|Luke 19:17], the faithful servant is rewarded with authority over ten cities because he was faithful in small things. This underscores the same thought as in Luke 16:12: faithfulness with what belongs to another (the master's money) leads to receiving something of one's own.

In [ref:1 Kor 4:2|1 Corinthians 4:2], Paul says that what is required of stewards is that they be found faithful. This is closely related to Luke 16:12, where faithfulness with what is foreign (another's property) is the condition for receiving what truly belongs to one.

In [ref:1 Pet 4:10|1 Peter 4:10], believers are urged to be good stewards of God's varied grace. What we steward belongs to God (it is "another's"), and our faithfulness with this determines what we receive as our own – in line with the principle in Luke 16:12.

In [ref:Luk 12:42-44|Luke 12:42-44], Jesus speaks of the faithful and wise steward whom the master puts in charge of all his possessions. Faithful management of what belongs to the master (what is foreign) is rewarded with being placed over all the master's goods – a parallel to the principle in Luke 16:12.

In [ref:Matt 6:19-21|Matthew 6:19-21], Jesus distinguishes between earthly treasures and heavenly treasures. Luke 16:12 distinguishes between what is foreign (temporal, earthly goods) and "what is your own" (true, eternal riches), reflecting this contrast.
